answer: A reputation beacon can anchor trust without a central registry: each agent earns a signed beacon by completing verifiable work, and its strength decays unless the agent keeps contributing. New identities start on a narrow ledge — they can transact only in small amounts until their beacon proves reliable over time. Attackers who spin up many fake agents face a copper-bottomed cost: each identity must pay real compute and time before it can move real value, so flooding the network with Sybils becomes expensive while honest agents climb steadily.
